_about: Short safety and how-to notes shown by safeNote(key) in src/app/01-core.js. Keep each text under about 30 words. Labs and lessons pick one with "safety": key or [keys]. tone good = reassurance (green), warn = a real-life caution (amber).

sim.title: Is this safe? Yes.
sim.text: This is a simulator. Commands run inside this page only, never on your computer or any network, so you can't break anything. Reset starts it again.

terminal: Click the dark box and type a command, such as ls, then press Enter.
Type help to list the commands, or man and a command's name to learn one.
Flags combine (ls -la), and Ubuntu's shortcuts work: ll is ls -alF.
Press ↑ to bring back an earlier command and Tab to finish a file name.
Stuck? Show a hint under the objectives, or Reset lab.
nettools: Click the dark box and type a command, such as ping, then press Enter.
Type help to list the commands, or man and a command's name to learn one.
Use the options you know from Linux or Windows: ping -c 4, ping -n 4, dig +short, ip a.
Press ↑ to bring back an earlier command and Tab to finish a word.
Stuck? Show a hint under the objectives, or Reset lab.
vlan: Pick a switch, router or PC above the console. Each has its own command line.
Type a command and press Enter. On a switch or router, a ? lists what can come next: try show ? to see everything show can display.
Shorthand works as on real Cisco kit: sh vl br, conf t, int f0/11, no shut, wr.
Press ↑ to bring back an earlier command and Tab to finish a word.
Stuck? Show a hint under the objectives, or Reset lab.
perms: Pick a file, then flip its switches or change the owner and group.
Or type commands such as ls -l and chmod in the dark box and press Enter.
Shortcuts work too: ll, chmod -R, chown user:group, and symbolic modes such as u+x.
The table shows who can read, change and run the file as you go.
Stuck? Show a hint under the objectives, or Reset lab.

sim.phone: Tap the line at the bottom of the dark box to bring up the keyboard, and use its Return key to run a command.

scan.title: Reading this is fine. Doing it for real needs permission.
scan.text: Scanning or probing computers you don't own, without written permission, can be a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, and similar laws elsewhere. Here you only read the results.

items: Scan only devices you own, on your own network.
Or use targets made for it: the Nmap Project lets you scan scanme.nmap.org (gently, not over and over), and practice sites such as TryHackMe and Hack The Box give you machines to attack.
At work, get a written scope and permission first, every time.

link.label: Practise reading a scope in the rules of engagement lab

osint.title: Looking is legal. Using it against people isn't.
osint.text: OSINT uses what anyone can see. Practise on yourself, or on your organisation with permission. Never use it to track, expose or pressure a real person.

items: Search for yourself: your name, usernames and email address, to see what others could find.
Don't log in to anything that isn't yours, guess passwords or message people under a false name.
Stalking, harassment and publishing someone's details to target them are crimes, even when the details were public.

paste.title: Is it OK to paste real data?
paste.text: It stays in this browser tab: nothing is uploaded or saved, and it's gone when you leave the page.

items: Check your employer's rules. Some data mustn't be copied anywhere, even onto your own screen.
Take out what you don't need: passwords, tokens, session cookies, and customers' names or email addresses.
Remove internal server names and addresses before you share a screenshot.
This tool never says something is safe. It shows what the evidence says, and you decide.

cvss.title: Nothing leaves this page.
cvss.text: The vector is decoded in your browser. It's added to the page's address so you can share a link; vectors aren't secret, advisories publish them.

progress.title: Where your progress lives
progress.text: Only in this browser, on this device. There's no account, no server and no sync, so nobody else can see it.

more.summary: What can lose it, and what's in a backup
items: Clearing your browsing history or site data deletes it.
Private or incognito windows forget it when you close them.
Another browser or device starts fresh: restore a code or file there.
A backup holds only your progress and settings: no name, email address or password.

install.title: Use it like an app (optional)
install.text: Installing from your browser gives Patch Notes its own window and lets pages you've opened work offline. It asks for no extra permissions.

items: Chrome or Edge on a computer: the install icon at the right of the address bar, or the browser's menu.
Android (Chrome): menu ⋮, then Add to Home screen or Install app.
iPhone or iPad (Safari): Share, then Add to Home Screen. The app keeps its own progress, separate from Safari, so move it across with a progress code.
Uninstalling can delete what the app saved, so back up first.

fictional.title: Real techniques, made-up people.
fictional.text: Every client, person and company in a shift is fictional, and the public IP addresses come from ranges kept for examples. The attacks and logs follow how real ones look.

cve.title: These are real flaws.
cve.text: Use this list to decide what to patch. Never try an exploit on a system you don't own or have written permission to test.

feedback.title: What gets sent
feedback.text: Only what you fill in here. Formspree, a form service, emails it to the site owner. Your email address goes only if you type it. Nothing is saved in your browser.

items: Like any website you send something to, Formspree sees your IP address.
Don't include passwords or anything you'd rather keep private.

examdate.text: Saved only in this browser, with your progress.

webattack.title: Safe here. On a real site it needs permission.
webattack.text: This shop is fictional and runs in your browser. Trying injection on a website you don't own, without written permission, can be a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

items: Run a deliberately vulnerable app on your own computer, such as OWASP Juice Shop.
Use free training labs made for it, such as PortSwigger's Web Security Academy.
At work, get written authorisation and an agreed scope before testing anything.
